name: Dog Show
description: A new dog show on TV is starting next week. On the show dogs are required to demonstrate bottomless stomach, strategic thinking and self-preservation instinct. You and your dog are invited to compete with other participants and naturally you want to win! On the show a dog needs to eat as many bowls of dog food as possible (bottomless stomach helps here). Dogs compete separately of each other and the rules are as follows: At the start of the show the dog and the bowls are located on a line. The dog starts at position x = 0 and n bowls are located at positions x = 1, x = 2, ..., x = n . The bowls are numbered from 1 to n from left to right. After the show starts the dog immediately begins to run to the right to the first bowl. The food inside bowls is not ready for eating at the start because it is too hot (dog's self-preservation instinct prevents eating). More formally, the dog can eat from the i -th bowl after t i seconds from the start of the show or later. It takes dog 1 second to move from the position x to the position x + 1 . The dog is not allowed to move to the left, the dog runs only to the right with the constant speed 1 distance unit per second. When the dog reaches a bowl (say, the bowl i ), the following cases are possible: the food had cooled down (i.e. it passed at least t i seconds from the show start): the dog immediately eats the food and runs to the right without any stop, the food is hot (i.e. it passed less than t i seconds from the show start): the dog has two options: to wait for the i -th bowl, eat the food and continue to run at the moment t i or to skip the i -th bowl and continue to run to the right without any stop. After T seconds from the start the show ends. If the dog reaches a bowl of food at moment T the dog can not eat it. The show stops before T seconds if the dog had run to the right of the last bowl. You need to help your dog create a strategy with which the maximum possible number of bowls of food will be eaten in T seconds.
input_specification: Two integer numbers are given in the first line - n and T ( 1 ≤ n ≤ 200 000 , 1 ≤ T ≤ 2·10 9 ) — the number of bowls of food and the time when the dog is stopped. On the next line numbers t 1 , t 2 , ..., t n ( 1 ≤ t i ≤ 10 9 ) are given, where t i is the moment of time when the i -th bowl of food is ready for eating.
output_specification: Output a single integer — the maximum number of bowls of food the dog will be able to eat in T seconds.
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 847D — Dog Show [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
